title: The Judiciary & Judicial Review
hook: Courts don't just settle disputes between people — through judicial review, many can also strike down a law or an official act that violates the constitution.
key_points: The judiciary interprets the law and resolves disputes by applying rules to specific cases.
Judicial review is the power of courts to invalidate laws or acts that conflict with the constitution.
Judicial independence — secure tenure, insulation from politics — lets courts rule against the powerful.
Not every country gives courts this power; where it exists, courts become a major check on the other branches.
content_html: The judiciary is the branch that interprets the law and resolves disputes — between individuals, between citizens and the state, or between branches of government — by applying general rules to specific facts. Its everyday work is adjudication: deciding who is right under the law in a particular case. But in many systems the courts hold a more far-reaching power as well.
extra_html: That power is judicial review: the authority to declare a law or an official act invalid when it conflicts with the constitution. Where it exists, it makes the judiciary a genuine check on the other branches, able to halt even a popularly enacted law if it violates higher constitutional rules. As Encyclopaedia Britannica explains, the practice spread widely after early courts asserted it, though not every country grants courts this role — some leave constitutional questions to the legislature or to special tribunals. For judicial review to mean anything, courts must be independent: judges need secure tenure and insulation from political retaliation so they can rule against even the most powerful officials. Judicial independence is therefore not a perk for judges but a structural condition for the rule of law itself.

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: Checks and Balances
related.hook: Separating power isn't enough — each branch also gets tools to limit the others, so power keeps power in check.

related.title: The Rule of Law
related.hook: The principle that everyone — including those in power — is bound by the same publicly known laws, applied equally.

related.title: What a Constitution Is
related.hook: The rulebook above the rules: a constitution sets out how a government is structured and the limits on its power.

related.title: When Judges Step Aside
related.hook: A judge who might be biased is supposed to step aside. But on the U.S. Supreme Court, each justice decides that alone — and no one can overrule them.

related.title: How the Supreme Court Decides a Case
related.hook: A top court hears only a sliver of the cases that beg for its attention — and the path from petition to ruling runs through written briefs, a public argument, and a vote taken in secret.

flashcards.prompt: What is the core function of the judiciary?

choices.text: To interpret the law and resolve disputes by applying rules to specific cases
To draft and pass new legislation
To run government ministries and agencies

flashcards.explanation_html: Courts apply the law to particular disputes; making law is the legislature's job and administering it is the executive's.

flashcards.prompt: Why does judicial independence matter for judicial review to work?

choices.text: Judges insulated from political pressure can rule against powerful officials
It lets judges write their own laws freely
It guarantees the government always wins its cases

flashcards.explanation_html: Secure tenure and insulation from politics let courts strike down even a government's acts without fear of reprisal.
